questions.prompt: What is the unit of electric potential?
questions.answer:
The unit of electric potential is the volt:
\[
1\,\mathrm{V}=1\,\mathrm{J\,C^{-1}}
\]

questions.prompt: Is electric potential a scalar or a vector?
State the relation between \(\Delta U\), \(q\), and \(\Delta V\).
A \(+4.0\,\mathrm{nC}\) charge moves through \(\Delta V=+25\,\mathrm{V}\). Find \(\Delta U\).
A \(-3.0\,\mu\mathrm{C}\) charge moves through \(\Delta V=+12\,\mathrm{V}\). Find \(\Delta U\).
A charge \(+2.0\,\mathrm{nC}\) moves from \(80\,\mathrm{V}\) to \(30\,\mathrm{V}\). Find the work done by the electric force.
questions.answer:
The potential change is
\[
\Delta V=V_f-V_i=30-80=-50\,\mathrm{V}
\]
Electric work is
\[
W_{\mathrm{elec}}=-q\Delta V
\]
\[
W_{\mathrm{elec}}=-(2.0\times10^{-9})(-50)
\]
\[
W_{\mathrm{elec}}=1.0\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm{J}
\]

questions.prompt: Find the potential \(0.25\,\mathrm{m}\) from a \(-6.0\,\mathrm{nC}\) point charge, using \(V(\infty)=0\).
An electron moves through a potential drop of \(15\,\mathrm{V}\). Determine the sign of its \(\Delta U\) and the sign of the electric work.
questions.answer:
A potential drop of \(15\,\mathrm{V}\) means
\[
\Delta V=-15\,\mathrm{V}
\]
For an electron, \(q=-e\). Therefore
\[
\Delta U=q\Delta V=(-e)(-15\,\mathrm{V})>0
\]
The electric work is
\[
W_{\mathrm{elec}}=-\Delta U<0
\]
So the electron's potential energy increases and the electric force does negative work for that specified displacement.

questions.prompt: A particle of charge \(q\) and mass \(m\) starts from rest and moves through a potential difference \(\Delta V\). Derive its final speed when electric work is the only work, including the condition on \(q\Delta V\) for the motion to be possible from rest.
questions.answer:
Electric work is
\[
W_{\mathrm{elec}}=-q\Delta V
\]
Starting from rest, the kinetic-energy change is
\[
\Delta K=\frac12 mv^2
\]
If electric work is the only work,
\[
\frac12 mv^2=-q\Delta V
\]
so
\[
v=\sqrt{\frac{-2q\Delta V}{m}}
\]
This motion from rest is possible only if
\[
-q\Delta V\ge0
\]
or
\[
q\Delta V\le0
\]
because the final kinetic energy cannot be negative.

questions.prompt: Two particles with charges \(+e\) and \(-e\) are each released from rest through the same potential difference from point A to point B. Derive the relation between their kinetic-energy changes and explain why one release may require reversing the direction of travel.
questions.answer:
For a displacement from A to B,
\[
\Delta K=-q\Delta V
\]
For \(+e\),
\[
\Delta K_+=-e\Delta V
\]
For \(-e\),
\[
\Delta K_-=-(-e)\Delta V=+e\Delta V
\]
Thus
\[
\Delta K_-=-\Delta K_+
\]
For the same directed potential difference, only one of the two signs gains kinetic energy from rest unless \(\Delta V=0\). To have both particles accelerate from rest under electric work alone, one must move through the opposite potential difference, meaning the direction of travel must be reversed for one charge sign.
